standard.title: Choosing Data Displays
standard.description: choose appropriate forms of display or visualisation for a given type of data; justify selections and interpret displays for a given context
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can represent and compare multiple data distributions using comparative representations (AC9M9ST03). They have not yet systematically matched display type to data type and purpose, or justified visualisation choices for a given audience and context.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students choose appropriate data displays for given data types, justify their selections, and interpret displays in context.

nodes.label: Matching display type to data type
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the data type (categorical nominal/ordinal, numerical discrete/continuous) and select an appropriate display type.
nodes.minimum_width: Classify one data set as categorical or numerical, discrete or continuous; select and justify an appropriate display type for it.
nodes.typical_width: Classify a range of data sets by type; match display types to data types (bar chart for categorical nominal, histogram for numerical continuous, dot plot or stem-and-leaf for small discrete numerical data sets); justify choices based on data type.
wider: Investigate non-standard display types such as infographics and assess what data type and purpose they are suited for — evaluate one real infographic
Compare the same data displayed in two different but plausible formats and evaluate which communicates more effectively for the intended audience
Use digital tools including generative AI to produce multiple display options for the same data set and critically evaluate each

response_modes.reason: Students commonly apply bar charts to all categorical data and histograms to all numerical data, without distinguishing discrete vs continuous or nominal vs ordinal. Working across a range of data types — including ordinal categorical (survey scales), numerical discrete (count data) and numerical continuous (measurement data) — builds accurate discrimination.

success_criteria: Correctly classifies the data type as categorical (nominal/ordinal) or numerical (discrete/continuous)
Selects an appropriate display type and names it
Justifies the selection with reference to the data type
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot classify data type (categorical vs numerical, discrete vs continuous) cannot make justified display choices in N2 — justification requires naming the data type as the reason.

nodes.label: Justifying and interpreting displays in context
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can justify a display choice with reference to purpose and audience, and interpret key features of a display in context.
nodes.minimum_width: Choose a display for a given data set and purpose; justify the choice with reference to both the data type and the audience; interpret one key feature of the display in context.
nodes.typical_width: Choose and justify display types for a range of contexts, considering data type, audience and purpose; interpret displays by identifying and explaining key features (trend, centre, spread, proportion) in context; compare and interpret stacked bar charts, area charts and line graphs for part-whole and trend data.
wider: Evaluate a non-standard visualisation (e.g. infographic from a news source) — assess purpose, audience and how well it communicates the statistical question
Use generative AI to produce display options for a data set, then critically evaluate which form is most appropriate for the intended purpose and audience
Investigate how stacked bar charts and area charts represent part-whole relationships and when line graphs are more appropriate for trend data

response_modes.reason: Justifying display choices requires integrating data type knowledge, audience awareness and purpose — not just selecting a graph type in isolation. Students who can classify data but cannot articulate why a display works for a specific audience and purpose have not reached the descriptor's full demand.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Non-standard visualisations (infographics, area charts, interactive displays) provide rich material for developing both statistical literacy and critical thinking. Students who evaluate real-world visualisations develop a transferable skill that spans data literacy, media literacy and civic reasoning.
success_criteria: Justifies a display choice with reference to both data type and purpose/audience
Correctly interprets at least two features of the display in the language of the context
Evaluates whether the display communicates the key message clearly and fairly
